title: Perspectives and challenges in circularly polarized luminescence of lanthanide(III) complexes: From solution-based systems to solid-state applications
claim: Solid-state CPL of Ln(III) materials is prone to artifacts from linear polarization, sample anisotropy, excitation geometry, polarizer reflections, and the sample’s own circular dichroism, so an isotropic or carefully corrected measurement is required before a glum value is trusted.
explanation: Commercial CPL is reliable for isotropic solutions. Ordered solids such as single crystals are said to need Stokes–Mueller correction, while powders in KBr or polymers should be rotated about the excitation axis and measured at several angles. Practical mitigations include unpolarized excitation, horizontal sample mounting, low-birefringence optics, high-resolution monochromators, and KBr dispersion. Printing and devices also demand thermal stability near 150 °C, which many molecular complexes lack.
scope: Solid films, crystals, pellets, and polymer dispersions of CPL-active Ln(III) compounds.
conditions: Distinguish highly ordered samples from randomly oriented powders or polymer films.
caveats: Artifact suppression reduces but does not eliminate experimental deviation; multiple spectra are still required. The review does not provide a universal correction protocol beyond pointing to the Stokes–Mueller literature.
